children: , the commercial and military engine manufacturer, agreed to buy Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75 billion Tuesday, tightening its grip on a critical engine-production bottleneck. GE shares gained approximately 0.3% to $338.285 during morning trading.

CPP produces precision castings for jet engines, missiles and power-generation turbines, with commercial and defense engines generating about 70% of its revenue. GE expects airfoil demand to climb more than 30% by 2030 and plans to fund the acquisition with cash and new debt. The strategic appeal is clear: owning more of the supply chain could help GE push engines out faster as aerospace demand races ahead of industry capacity.

The purchase price represents 26 times projected 2027 EBITDA before integration benefits and 18 times afterward, implying roughly $200 million in expected annual gains. It also equals nearly four times GE's $3 billion of second-quarter free cash flow. The valuation picture adds another warning: GE trades 24.74% above its $271.19 GF Value estimate, leaving little room for execution mistakes. Buying the bottleneck could unlock production, but GE must expand CPP without disrupting third-party customers or turning an expensive solution into a new operational headache.

title: GE Aerospace Gains After Paying 26 Times Profit for a Bottleneck
